newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition vows town hall takeovers.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition vows town hall takeovers.

text.p: Opposition leaders vowed on Saturday to take control of big towns won from the ruling socialists in disputed elections that have sparked two weeks of huge demonstrations against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties said it would try to take over town halls on Monday although official results are still pending in some towns and fresh rounds of voting will be held in others to sort out the chaos.
Zajedno claimed it had won in Novi Sad, Uzice, Kikinda, Kragujevac, Cacak, Pirot and Zranjanin, ending more than 50 years of unbroken communist or socialist rule.

At least 100,000 people demonstrated in Belgrade on Saturday against socialist attempts to overturn the outcome of voting this month which gave Zajedno victory in most big towns including Belgrade and Nis.
The socialists annulled the results in the capital and Nis and regained control in fresh ballots amid a two-week campaign of street protests demanding Milosevic's ouster.

Zajedno leader Vesna Pesic told a news conference on Saturday: "This is not just a one-time protest but the beginning of the end of this totalitarian regime and it has to end with democracy in Serbia."
Marchers in Belgrade pelted state-controlled Serbian television with fruit, paint and eggs and smoke bombs but stewards ensured there was no violence.
The number of protesters, including parents with young children, grew despite doubts that peaceful demonstrations could break Milosevic's grip on power.
Large reserves of police were marshalled in the city as the two-week protest continued but stayed out of sight and Milosevic maintained his public silence.
One mother said she brought her children "because I want them to learn what democracy is...I want them to remember this."
The demonstrations are the longest sustained popular challenge to Milosevic's nine-year rule during which he has presided over the breakup of former Yugoslavia and wars with Croatia and Bosnia.
With both sides bidding for the support of the wider public in Serbia, the opposition and student leaders want to deprive the authorities of any opportunity to accuse them of violence.

They have been made vulnerable since Zajedno leader Danica Draskovic was heard telling reporters she would like to see the emergence of terrorism as Zajedno said the election fraud showed that Milosevic could not be removed by fair elections.

Zoran Djindjic, another opposition leader told a news conference on Saturday: "All the towns where we have won a majority will be organised as free municipalities. These will legal, democratic authorities opposed to the totalitarian regime in the municipalities where (socialists) won."
Opposition parties are threatening to boycott parliament and local councils unless Serbia's parliament cancels the disputed election results when it meets on Tuesday.
A boycott would have little practical effect because the socialists control the republican and federal parliaments.
But opposition leaders believe it would underscore their campaign to convince the world that Milosevic runs a one-party state despite the appearance of multi-party democracy in Yugoslavia.
Diplomats said Milosevic, whose police force has kept a low profile, hoped the demonstration campaign across the country would run out of steam.
Privately Zajedno officials agree that they will probably not win any substantial victory, but insist their tactics have uncovered cracks in his power.
"We have torn off his mask in front of the world to show him as he really is -- a small-time Balkan dictator unable to bear the slightest defeat," Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said.
